question: Tell me about a time you delivered work that was fit for purpose and nothing more. How did you decide where to stop?

raiseTranscript.text: I was asked to build a simple internal dashboard for tracking ticket volume. The request came with a tight deadline so I used an existing template and added only the three charts the manager had explicitly asked for.
How did you decide what to leave out?
I listed every possible chart we could add and crossed off anything that wasn't mentioned in the original ask. I also checked with my mentor who confirmed we could iterate later if needed.
The dashboard went live in two days instead of the planned week. My manager used it immediately and later asked for one extra filter which I added in an hour.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you delivered work that was fit for purpose and nothing more. How did you decide where to stop?
Built internal ticket dashboard using existing template; limited to three requested charts
Decided scope by listing extras and crossing them off; confirmed with mentor
Quote: 'I crossed off anything that wasn't mentioned in the original ask'
Follow-up: Asked how they validated the cutoff; candidate described quick check with mentor and willingness to iterate
Outcome: Live in two days; one follow-up request handled in an hour
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Scrappy, not crappy. The candidate described scoping a dashboard to exactly the three charts requested and shipping in two days by reusing a template. They explicitly listed possible additions then removed them after confirming with a mentor. This shows early understanding of stopping criteria tied to the original request rather than personal preference. The follow-up request was handled quickly, reinforcing that iteration was acceptable. Biggest strength is the concrete mechanism used to decide what to cut.

lowerTranscript.text: I built a full analytics page with ten different visualizations even though the team only needed volume trends.
I thought it would be more useful and I wanted to show what I could do.
Not directly, but I assumed they would want them later.

junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Scrappy, not crappy. The candidate added ten visualizations without being asked and justified it by assuming future need and wanting to showcase skills. No mechanism was described for deciding where to stop. This produced unnecessary work on an individual task. The gap is lack of any scoping discipline tied to the stated request.

raiseTranscript.text: Our partner team needed a basic integration to pull order status. Instead of a full bidirectional sync I proposed a one-way nightly export that met their SLA.
How did you align on scope?
I ran a 30-minute meeting with their tech lead, listed three options with effort estimates, and we picked the lightest one that still hit their reporting deadline.
They went live on schedule. Two months later they asked for real-time updates and we upgraded the integration with the data we had from the first version.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you delivered work that was fit for purpose and nothing more. How did you decide where to stop?

Outcome: On-time launch; later upgrade used data from initial version
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Scrappy, not crappy. The candidate limited a cross-team integration to a one-way nightly export after running a short scoping meeting that produced three options and a joint decision. Scope was tied directly to the partner's SLA rather than building a full sync. The later upgrade request was handled efficiently because the initial version already existed. Biggest strength is the repeatable process used to align two teams on minimal scope.

lowerTranscript.text: I pushed for a full real-time bidirectional sync because I knew it would be better long-term.
Did the partner ask for real-time?
No, but I wanted to avoid technical debt.
The project slipped by three weeks and the partner had to adjust their launch date.

Follow-up: Asked about partner request; candidate admitted real-time was not asked for
Outcome: Three-week slip and partner launch delay
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Scrappy, not crappy. The candidate expanded scope to a full bidirectional sync without partner request, citing future technical debt. No joint scoping discussion occurred. The result was a three-week delay that affected the partner team. The gap is prioritizing personal technical preferences over the stated cross-team need.

raiseTranscript.text: We needed to enter a new market in six weeks. I approved a stripped-down launch using only the core checkout flow and existing payment providers.
How did you decide the cutoff?

I asked each function lead for their minimum viable feature list, then removed anything that didn't directly enable the first 100 customers. We documented the trade-offs in a one-page memo to the leadership team.
We hit the market window. Revenue started at 60 percent of the full plan but we added the next set of features in the following quarter using actual usage data.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you delivered work that was fit for purpose and nothing more. How did you decide where to stop?

Collected minimum lists from function leads then cut anything not enabling first 100 customers

Follow-up: How trade-offs were communicated; candidate described explicit one-page memo and usage-driven follow-up
Outcome: Hit market window; later features added from real usage data
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Scrappy, not crappy. The executive limited a market launch to a core checkout flow by collecting minimum requirements from each function and cutting everything not required for the first 100 customers. Trade-offs were captured in a single memo for leadership visibility. The approach produced an on-time entry with follow-on features guided by actual data. Biggest strength is the org-level scoping process that balanced speed and later iteration.

lowerTranscript.text: I insisted we launch with the full feature set including advanced recommendations and new payment rails.
Why include those on day one?
I believed a premium experience was required to compete.
We missed the target window by eight weeks and entered after two competitors.

No minimum scoping exercise occurred. The result was an eight-week delay and lost first-mover advantage. The gap is absence of any mechanism to align the organization on the smallest viable entry.
